new_statements.quote: Les accents sont ceux du quôc ngü annamite. Pourtant les tons ne semblent pas bien fixés et varient pour certains mots d'un individu à l'autre. Il faut ajouter que la langue diffère un peu suivant les groupements. Par exemple les Lati de Man P'ang ne parlent pas tout à fait comme ceux de Ban Phung ou de Tou Long Xin Kai. Le vocabulaire ci-après a été pris à Man P'ang. [p.347 Nota: Ici l'accent aigu est réservé à l'indication du ton aigu.] (archive.org text layer reads 'Ban Phurig', '11 faut')
new_statements.translation: The diacritics are those of Annamite quoc-ngu. Yet the tones do not seem well fixed and vary, for certain words, from one individual to another. One must add that the language differs a little between settlements; for instance the Lati of Man P'ang do not speak quite like those of Ban Phung or Tou Long Xin Kai. The vocabulary below was taken down at Man P'ang. [Nota: here the acute accent is reserved for marking the high tone.]
new_statements.citation: Robert, G. 1913. Notice sur les Lati. Revue d'ethnographie et de sociologie 4 (9-12): 338-352. Paris: Leroux. (Glottolog 'Robert, M. 1916'; Ostapirat 2000 'Robert, J. 1913'; the running head of his 1914 sequel gives the initial G.)
new_statements.locator: p.343 ('Langue'), immediately before the page break to 344; Nota on p.347
new_statements.relation_note: Tonal (tones transcribed with quoc-ngu marks, judged 'not well fixed'); no stress statement anywhere in the notice.
new_statements.rule_in_words: White Lachi of Man P'ang is recorded as a tone language (tones written with Vietnamese quoc-ngu diacritics; acute = high tone), with the observer noting inter-speaker variation in the tones of some words; nothing is said about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.identity_note: p.343: 'Le vocabulaire ci-après a été pris à Man P'ang' - Man P'ang = Bản Pắng, the White (Central) Lachi village of Ostapirat 2000 / Edmondson 2008; Robert explicitly contrasts it with Ban Phung (Long-haired Lachi) and Tou Long Xin Kai. | p.271: the La-ti families are at Ban-phung (38), Ban-diu (30) and Ban-pang (8); pp.274-275: the wordlist was dictated by three La-ti men, one a village chief, village not stated. Ostapirat 2000:35 judges Bonifacy's forms to pattern with Ban Pang (Central = White Lachi); identity with whit1266 is therefore probable, not certain.

new_statements.quote: On voit, par ce vocabulaire, que le la-ti ne possède pas d'explosive finale, que sa forme est monosyllabique et variotone, [...] On peut encore noter la fréquence de la labiale nasale m combinée avec une autre consonne et l'existence de quatre tons seulement. (tesseract scanned of the Persée page images reads 'la-{i', 'par d'explosive', 'variolone', 'avee', 'Pexistence')
new_statements.translation: One sees from this vocabulary that La-ti has no final stop, that its form is monosyllabic and tonal ('variotone') ... One may further note the frequency of the labial nasal m combined with another consonant, and the existence of only four tones.
new_statements.citation: Bonifacy, Auguste. 1906. Étude sur les coutumes et la langue des La-ti. Bulletin de l'École française d'Extrême-Orient 6: 271-278. doi:10.3406/befeo.1906.4258
new_statements.locator: p.277, paragraph after the numerals, before 'Syntaxe'
new_statements.relation_note: Tone only: 'variotone', 'quatre tons seulement'; nothing on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: La-ti is described as monosyllabic and tonal with only four tones and no final stops; no remark on stress or accent.
new_statements.identity_note: p.343: 'Le vocabulaire ci-après a été pris à Man P'ang' - Man P'ang = Bản Pắng, the White (Central) Lachi village of Ostapirat 2000 / Edmondson 2008; Robert explicitly contrasts it with Ban Phung (Long-haired Lachi) and Tou Long Xin Kai. | p.271: the La-ti families are at Ban-phung (38), Ban-diu (30) and Ban-pang (8); pp.274-275: the wordlist was dictated by three La-ti men, one a village chief, village not stated. Ostapirat 2000:35 judges Bonifacy's forms to pattern with Ban Pang (Central = White Lachi); identity with whit1266 is therefore probable, not certain.

sources.note: Describes Long-haired Lachi (Tan Loi hamlet < Ban Phung) = lach1248, NOT White Lachi: Intro p.1 says the Ban Pang / Ban May (White Lachi) villages 'seem to have already abandoned their mother tongue and came to speak Nung'; ch.6.3 (pp.131-136) uses only Lachi (K) and Jinchang (LJC), no Ban Pang data. Its stress remarks (ch.1 pp.7-9, 23, 28: phrase/word-final 'major' syllable carries full stress and tone, preceding minor syllables reduced; 'stress-placing tendency is of rear-ward nature') therefore apply to lach1248 only.
